chosen.title: One Brain, Many Bodies: How Robot Foundation Models Learned to Move the Whole Machine
chosen.rationale: Google DeepMind's just-shipped Gemini Robotics 2 moves from tabletop upper-body tasks to true whole-body control, and its 'motion transfer' lets one learned policy adapt to a brand-new robot body in a few hours with under 200 examples — the mechanism-rich, embodied-AI story Kenji owns, and distinct from AIMA's existing IPO/factory-floor/world-model robot pieces.

sources.name: Google DeepMind — Gemini Robotics 2 brings whole body intelligence to robots
The Robot Report — DeepMind says Gemini Robotics 2 enables full body control

rejected_candidates.title: Printing the Unprintable: How Green Lasers Finally Cracked Copper for the AI Hardware Boom
rejected_candidates.rationale: 2026 is a genuine inflection point for metal additive manufacturing: green-laser powder-bed fusion now prints pure copper at 99.8% density — the material behind the liquid cold plates cooling AI accelerators — plus gold, silver, and space-grade parts, with AI-driven process control making it production-ready. A sensory, build-it-yourself manufacturing/materials piece squarely in Kenji's wheelhouse, and untouched by the autonomous-lab and robotic-aerospace articles already covered.

sources.name: 3Dnatives — Green laser enables 3D printing of pure copper and copper alloys
TCT Magazine — Big metal 3D printing and lots of laser power: TCT Asia 2026

rejected_candidates.title: Eyes That Never Blink: How AI Is Turning a Flood of Satellite Data Into a Living Map of Earth
rejected_candidates.rationale: Private Earth-observation constellations (spotlighted at Small Satellite 2026) are generating more imagery than any human team can read, and AI is now the only way to make sense of the glut — powering climate and disaster monitoring while raising real surveillance and access risks. It sits at Kenji's aerospace + climate-tech + AI intersection and doesn't overlap AIMA's orbital-data-center or consumer-surveillance pieces.

sources.name: Space.com — The future of Earth observation: private satellites and AI bring benefits but also pose risks
